cards.explanation: The answer is that his speeches serve no purpose. Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends, asks, “Should he argue with useless words or speeches that serve no purpose?” (Job 15:3). So he is calling Job's speeches empty. That's a rough review, friends, and I'd be hiding behind my mixing bowl right about now.

The answer is mouth. Eliphaz says, “Your own mouth, not mine, condemns you; your own lips testify against you.” (Job 15:6). He is pointing at what Job has said. Mouth and lips both do the testifying, so Job's own words are the witness here.

The answer is that Job knows nothing they don't. Eliphaz asks, “What do you know that we do not? What do you understand that is not clear to us?” (Job 15:9). Before that he asks whether Job listens in on God's council or limits wisdom to himself. He is saying Job has no secret knowledge. It's a bold thing to say to a man in Job's spot.

The answer is True. Eliphaz says, “Both the gray-haired and the aged are on our side—men much older than your father.” He is lining up a whole row of elders behind him. I think he wants Job to feel outnumbered by experience.

The answer is that Job is turning his spirit against God. Eliphaz asks why Job's heart has carried him away and why his eyes flash, “…so that you turn your spirit against God and pour such words from your mouth?” (Job 15:12-13). That's what he accuses Job of. Those are Eliphaz's words about Job, and they land hard.

The answer is False. Eliphaz says, “If God puts no trust in His holy ones, if even the heavens are not pure in His eyes…” (Job 15:15). The words are about God putting no trust in His holy ones, the opposite of complete trust. Then he asks how much less man could measure up.

The word is injustice. Eliphaz says man is “…vile and corrupt, who drinks injustice like water?” (Job 15:16). Water is something people drink all the time, so that's a picture of injustice going down easy. It's a heavy way for Eliphaz to talk about people, friends.

The answer is a wicked man. Eliphaz says, “A wicked man writhes in pain all his days; only a few years are reserved for the ruthless.” (Job 15:20). He opens his teaching with the wicked man and stays on him to the end of the speech. Everything after this is what Eliphaz says happens to him.

The answer is False. Eliphaz says, “Sounds of terror fill his ears; in his prosperity the destroyer attacks him.” The attack comes in his prosperity, not after he's poor. So the trouble arrives while things look good.

The answer is that he stretched out his hand against God. Eliphaz says, “For he has stretched out his hand against God and has vaunted himself against the Almighty…” (Job 15:25). That's the reason he gives for the trouble. He puts it all on the man's stance toward God.

The answer is True. Eliphaz says the wicked man is “…rushing headlong at Him with a thick, studded shield.” (Job 15:26). That's a charging picture, and he's carrying heavy protection. It's the picture Eliphaz paints of someone running at the Almighty.

The word is ruined. Eliphaz says the wicked man “…will dwell in ruined cities, in abandoned houses destined to become rubble.” (Job 15:28). It's a picture of a man ending up in a broken-down place. Nobody is renting there, friends.

The answer is False. Eliphaz says, “He will no longer be rich; his wealth will not endure. His possessions will not overspread the land.” (Job 15:29). So the wealth won't last, and his possessions won't spread across the land. That's why the statement is false.

The answer is emptiness. Eliphaz says, “Let him not deceive himself with trust in emptiness, for emptiness will be his reward.” (Job 15:31). The word shows up twice, and he means it both times. Trust in empty things, and empty is what you get.

The answer is that he will not flourish. Eliphaz says, “…his branch will not flourish.” and then pictures “…a vine stripped of its unripe grapes…” and “…an olive tree that sheds its blossoms.” (Job 15:32-33). Both pictures show something losing what it was growing. That's the image he gives of the wicked man.

The word is evil. Eliphaz says, “They conceive trouble and give birth to evil; their womb is pregnant with deceit.” (Job 15:35). He pictures trouble starting and evil coming out of it. That's how he ends the speech, friends.
